data.name: Fairness can soften unfair rules
data.plainSummary: Sometimes applying a rule word-for-word produces an unfair outcome. Many frameworks hold that judges and lawmakers may soften rigid rules so concrete cases align better with justice.
data.whyRoot: Rules are written in advance for typical cases; life produces outliers. Without a safety valve for proportion and fairness, law becomes mechanical cruelty. Equity is a root because justice is not the same as a checklist.
data.description: Foundational claim drawn from Roman jurisprudence that aequitas—fairness and proportion—guides judges and lawmakers in tempering rigid rules so outcomes align with justice in concrete cases.

data.name: Bodily self-determination for competent adults
data.plainSummary: Competent adults should generally direct decisions about their own bodies, including medical choices, unless a strong overriding reason exists—such as serious harm to others.
data.whyRoot: The body is the medium through which a person experiences the world; if others controlled it by default, personal agency would mean little. Bodily authority is treated as a root because it pairs moral personhood with a zone of decision-making that others must justify crossing.
data.description: Foundational claim that competent adults have primary moral and legal authority over their own bodies, including medical choices, absent overriding harm to others.

data.name: Christian scripture and tradition as moral authority
data.plainSummary: Within Catholic and broader Christian moral theology, sacred scripture and the Church's teaching office (where accepted) supply norms for virtue, vice, and conscience.
data.whyRoot: For frameworks that take this stance, lists like the capital vices are not mere opinion: they classify recurring ways human willing goes wrong. The graph stops here for believers; others can still read the downstream principles as historically influential moral categories.
data.description: Foundational claim, for faith-based branches of the graph, that Christian scripture and ecclesial tradition (especially in Catholic and Orthodox moral theology) authoritatively frame the classification of serious moral failure, including the tradition of capital vices (deadly sins).

data.name: Coherent legal order
data.plainSummary: The framework holds that legal rules should fit together into a clear, coherent system—often worked out through careful reasoning and codes—rather than a messy pile of unrelated edicts.
data.whyRoot: People need to know what duties and rights they actually have. If law is a tangle of contradictions, planning and fairness collapse. Coherence is treated as foundational because predictable, unified rules are what let strangers coordinate without constant conflict.
data.description: Foundational civilian ideal that legal rules should form a coherent body, developed through reasoned commentary and (where appropriate) codification, traceable to Roman models of ordered private law and public authority.

data.name: Equal moral consideration
data.plainSummary: The framework holds that everyone who counts in the discussion should matter equally when weighing rights, burdens, and opportunities, unless a specific reason supports different treatment.
data.whyRoot: Arbitrary favoritism turns law into club rules. Starting from equal consideration forces reasons for unequal treatment into the open. It is a root because it blocks treating 'my group counts more' as a silent default.
data.description: Foundational claim that all persons (or all in a defined scope) deserve equal standing in moral and often legal reasoning about rights, burdens, and opportunities, absent specific differences that justify unequal treatment.

data.name: Evidence anchors high-stakes law and policy
data.plainSummary: When laws or rules seriously affect health, safety, or freedom, they should align with the best available evidence and expert consensus when that exists.
data.whyRoot: When mistakes are costly and hard to reverse, guessing is a poor basis for coercion. Anchoring high-stakes rules to the best shared picture of facts is a root commitment: it reduces arbitrary harm and makes public justification possible.
data.description: Foundational commitment that when laws or regulations materially affect health, safety, or liberty, they should align with credible empirical and expert consensus where such evidence exists.

data.name: Parties owe each other fair dealing
data.plainSummary: In bargains and ongoing legal relationships, the framework expects each side to treat the other fairly—not only to follow the letter of the contract while acting in a one-sided or exploitative way.
data.whyRoot: Bargaining assumes each party can count on something beyond gamesmanship. If only the bare form of words counted, clever abuse would win and cooperation would stay fragile. Fair dealing is a root commitment because it names the minimum mutual respect that makes long-term relationships workable.
data.description: Foundational commitment to reciprocal fairness in performance and enforcement: parties may not weaponize formal rights to surprise, oppress, or take advantage in ways civil-law and common-law systems often capture under abuse-of-right or good-faith doctrines.

data.name: Fidelity to the spirit of agreements
data.plainSummary: Once someone undertakes a commitment, the framework holds that they should stand by its purpose and reasonable expectations—not only the narrowest reading that benefits them.
data.whyRoot: Promises coordinate expectations over time. If people could always dodge the point of a deal whenever a loophole appeared, others could not rely on undertakings, and cooperation would stall. Fidelity to the bargain is foundational because it is what makes words actually binding in practice.
data.description: Foundational commitment to loyalty to the bargain (allied with pacta-related ideas in many traditions): performance and interpretation should respect the agreement's intent and the trust the other party reasonably placed in the undertaking.

data.name: Truthfulness in agreements and dealings
data.plainSummary: In legal and private relationships, people should tell the truth, avoid misleading others, and disclose what fairness requires—not exploit silence or fine print in bad faith.
data.whyRoot: Voluntary cooperation rests on a shared picture of reality: if people can lie or hide what matters, planning, exchange, and trust break down. Honesty is treated as a stopping point because without it, weaker parties are easy to manipulate and almost nothing else in private law can be relied on.
data.description: Foundational commitment that veracity and good-faith disclosure matter in forming, performing, and interpreting obligations; a building block for doctrines of fraud, misrepresentation, and implied duties in many legal systems.

data.name: Liberty as default; limits require justification
data.plainSummary: The framework holds that people should generally be free to choose for themselves. Restricting freedom calls for a substantive reason—such as preventing harm—rather than habit or preference alone.
data.whyRoot: Liberty is costly to restrict and easy to abuse: every constraint needs a public justification. This root flips the burden so freedom is presumed and interference must earn its place—so power cannot treat restriction as the default posture of government.
data.description: Foundational liberal or libertarian commitment that interference with voluntary choice requires a positive justification (harm prevention, consent of the governed, etc.), rather than the reverse.

data.name: Human life as intrinsically significant
data.plainSummary: Human life matters for its own sake—not only because it is useful. Many arguments about ethics and medicine start from this idea.
data.whyRoot: If life only mattered when it was convenient or productive, people could be discarded whenever costs rose. Treating human life as carrying weight on its own is a stopping point for a huge swath of medical and legal reasoning: it says persons are not mere instruments.
data.description: Foundational claim that human life is valuable in itself, often used as a root for autonomy and medical ethics arguments within many frameworks.

data.name: Reduce suffering
data.plainSummary: Morally, reducing pain and hardship (and often improving well-being) for everyone affected by a decision carries weight.
data.whyRoot: Suffering is the clearest signal that something is going wrong for a subject of experience. Many ethical systems stop here because once suffering counts, there is reason to weigh outcomes and side effects instead of treating people as props in someone else's story.
data.description: Classical utilitarian starting point: moral weight attaches to the reduction of suffering (and often the promotion of well-being) across those affected.

data.name: Basic moral truths are open to human reason
data.plainSummary: In the Thomistic family of views, people can often know—without special revelation—that certain actions are wrong or disordered, because they bear on human flourishing and justice.
data.whyRoot: If some moral structure is knowable in principle, then religious and secular interlocutors can still argue about vices, virtues, and law on overlapping ground. This axiom does not deny revelation; it marks a distinct stopping point for what reason alone is said to reach.
data.description: Foundational claim associated with classical natural-law theory (including Thomism): core requirements of practical reason—such as prohibitions on grave injustice and certain disordered acts—are in principle accessible through reflection on human nature and the common good, not only through scripture.

data.name: Prior decisions bind or strongly guide later ones
data.plainSummary: Prior court decisions should usually bind or strongly guide later decisions, so the law stays predictable—unless a compelling reason supports changing course.
data.whyRoot: Legal disputes are supposed to be settled by rules people could have seen coming. If every case started from scratch, law would be arbitrary and investment in cooperation would shrink. Precedent is a root commitment to stability and notice.
data.description: Foundational commitment that adjudication should be stable and predictable by treating prior court decisions as authoritative or highly persuasive absent compelling reason to depart—core to the Anglo-American common law tradition.

data.name: Preventable death requires strong justification
data.plainSummary: Frameworks that treat preventable death as unacceptable hold that when harm can be avoided through medicine, policy, or infrastructure, allowing it to occur requires a strong justification. That stance is common in public health and longevity-oriented worldviews.
data.whyRoot: When harm can be prevented at reasonable cost, letting it occur anyway normally requires a positive defense—otherwise neglect looks like a choice. This root ties the possibility of action to moral urgency rather than regret alone.
data.description: Foundational commitment that deaths avoidable through known means (medical, policy, or infrastructure) ought not to occur without strong justification; common in public-health and longevity-oriented frameworks.

data.name: A written constitution is the highest law
data.plainSummary: The framework holds that the basic rules of government belong in a written charter above ordinary laws: it divides power, sets up institutions, and limits what legislatures can do.
data.whyRoot: Power needs stable, public limits so people can plan their lives and hold rulers accountable. A supreme written charter is a root in this tradition because it makes those limits visible and harder to erase in a single ordinary vote.
data.description: Foundational commitment that political authority should be structured by a written charter that allocates powers, defines institutions, and stands above ordinary legislation—central to the U.S. federal order.

data.name: Contempt, obstruction, and abuse of legal process
data.description: Legal constructs punishing disrespect or defiance toward courts and lawful authority, false statements to investigators, and manipulation of procedure—loosely analogous to moral concerns about hubris, defiance of legitimate order, and contempt for truth in institutional settings.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Contempt powers vary; tension between dignity, free expression, and institutional authority is ongoing.

pros.claim: Protects the integrity of adjudication and investigation when cooperation and candor are essential.
pros.evidence: Obstruction and perjury-adjacent offenses are standard features of modern legal systems.

cons.claim: 'Pride' as a spiritual vice is only weakly correlated with legal contempt; dissent and civil disobedience raise distinct legitimacy questions.
cons.evidence: Political theory and constitutional law debate when defiance of authority is justified.

disobedience-legitimacy-debate.title: Civil disobedience and legal obligation — philosophical debate

data.name: Criminal force and violence against the person
data.description: Legal constructs governing assault, battery, homicide, and related offenses—where the state punishes unjustified injury or credible threats, often discussed alongside moral critiques of wrath and disproportionate anger.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Core of penal law everywhere; self-defense and proportionality doctrines differ by system.

pros.claim: Protects bodily integrity and public order through clear prohibitions on unlawful harm.
pros.evidence: Battery and assault statutes and common-law crimes form a stable cross-jurisdictional family.

cons.claim: Legal 'force' doctrines do not track spiritual 'wrath' perfectly; justified force and systemic violence raise separate questions.
cons.evidence: Policing, war, and self-defense carve out large exceptions that moral theology treats under different headings.

violence-offenses-overview.title: Offenses against the person — introductory survey

justified-force-boundaries.title: Self-defense, necessity, and justified force — legal and ethical boundaries

data.name: Fraud, theft, and wrongful appropriation
data.description: Legal constructs that prohibit acquiring or withholding another's property or entitlement through deception, stealth, or abuse of trust—often discussed alongside moral critiques of covetousness and envy.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Near-universal in legal systems; exact elements and defenses vary sharply by jurisdiction.

pros.claim: Gives institutional teeth to prohibitions on taking what is not one's due.
pros.evidence: Criminal and civil doctrines worldwide address theft, fraud, embezzlement, and conversion with overlapping rationales.

cons.claim: Moral categories like greed or envy do not map one-to-one onto legal labels; many thefts are impulsive or survival-driven.
cons.evidence: Sentencing and poverty debates show heterogeneous motives behind economically similar acts.

theft-fraud-model-overview.title: Theft and fraud — comparative criminal-law overview

motive-heterogeneity-note.title: Economic motive, need, and property offenses — criminological survey

data.name: Intoxication and substance-related offenses
data.description: Legal constructs addressing public drunkenness, driving under the influence, and controlled-substance rules—an imperfect but recurring legal analogue to moral warnings about intemperance and disordered appetite (including gluttony in its broader classical sense).
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Policy shifts between prohibition, harm reduction, and medical models complicate any simple moral mapping.

pros.claim: Targets acute public-safety risks from impaired judgment and coordination.
pros.evidence: DUI/DWI regimes and public-intoxication laws are widespread responses to measurable harms.

cons.claim: Gluttony as a spiritual vice is a poor fit for addiction science and socioeconomic drivers of substance use.
cons.evidence: Public-health literature distinguishes disease, dependence, and moral fault in ways classical vice lists did not.

dui-public-safety-rationale.title: Impaired driving law — public safety rationale and evaluation

addiction-vs-vice-framing.title: Addiction, responsibility, and criminal law — framing debates

data.name: Negligence and breach of duty of care
data.description: Private-law constructs imposing liability when a person fails to meet a standard of care owed to others—one legal analogue (among others) to moral blame for culpable omission or sloth, though civil negligence does not require spiritual apathy.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Common-law negligence and civilian analogues are well developed; standards of care remain fact-specific.

pros.claim: Translates avoidable carelessness into remediable harm without requiring criminal intent.
pros.evidence: Negligence dominates accident compensation in many jurisdictions.

cons.claim: Clinical depression, burnout, and structural overload undermine easy mapping from 'sloth' to legal breach.
cons.evidence: Disability and labor contexts show that non-performance often lacks moral blameworthiness.

negligence-standard-overview.title: The negligence standard — introductory treatise overview

capacity-and-breach-note.title: Capacity, mental health, and breach of duty — tort law perspectives

data.name: Right to access experimental therapy
data.description: Legal concept covering circumstances under which patients may access therapies not yet fully approved under ordinary regulatory pathways.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Depends heavily on jurisdiction-specific statutes and regulatory exceptions.

pros.claim: Can expand options for patients facing serious or life-threatening conditions.
pros.evidence: Expanded access and similar programs exist specifically to address urgent unmet medical need.

cons.claim: May expose patients to interventions with uncertain benefit-risk profiles.
cons.evidence: Early-phase evidence often does not establish efficacy; harm can still occur.

early-phase-evidence-limit.title: Clinical evidence limitations in early-phase trials

data.name: Sexual offenses, consent, and privacy
data.description: Legal constructs addressing non-consensual sexual acts, exploitation of incapacity, and privacy-related sexual wrongs—areas where modern law foregrounds autonomy and harm, while historical and religious moral language often emphasized lust and chastity.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Rapid legal and social change around consent, age, and digital harms; high contestation.

pros.claim: Centers consent and protection of vulnerable persons in ways many frameworks converge on.
pros.evidence: International human-rights instruments and national reforms increasingly align on consent-centric models.

cons.claim: Moral-theological 'lust' and legal 'lack of consent' are not coextensive; marriage law, obscenity, and morals offenses show persistent divergence.
cons.evidence: Jurisdictions differ on criminalization of adult consensual conduct and on sex work.

consent-reform-trends.title: Sexual offense law and consent — reform trends

morals-law-divergence.title: Moral regulation vs. harm principle in sexual offense law

data.name: Bodily autonomy
data.description: Derived principle: persons have substantial authority over what happens to their own bodies, including medical decisions.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Widely recognized in medical ethics and law, though boundaries remain contested at the edges.

pros.claim: Aligns with widely accepted informed consent frameworks in clinical practice.
pros.evidence: Informed consent is a standard requirement across modern healthcare systems.

cons.claim: May conflict with public health measures that require mandatory interventions.
cons.evidence: Vaccination mandates and quarantine powers illustrate recurring tension between autonomy and collective welfare.

public-health-tension-note.title: Public health vs. individual autonomy — introductory note

data.name: Good faith (bona fides) in private law
data.plainSummary: Roman private law ties these ideas together: honesty, fair dealing, and faithfulness to agreements—so obligations and interpretation are guided by bona fides, not bare formalism alone.
data.description: Synthesis principle from classical Roman jurisprudence: obligations, interpretation, and conduct in private law should be guided by bona fides—honesty, fair dealing, and loyalty to the bargain—rather than compliance with the letter alone.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Central to civilian systems and influential elsewhere; exact scope and institutional form vary by jurisdiction.

pros.claim: Aligns contract and property law with lived expectations of trust and cooperation.
pros.evidence: Good-faith standards appear across modern civil codes and influence common-law doctrines such as implied duties and unconscionability.

cons.claim: Open-ended good-faith language can create uncertainty about duties and liability.
cons.evidence: Debates over certainty vs. flexibility recur wherever courts imply obligations beyond express terms.

good-faith-uncertainty-note.title: Indeterminacy and good-faith standards — introductory note

data.name: Envy (invidia) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this tradition, envy is sorrow or resentment at another's good—wishing to lower them or possess what is theirs in a disordered way.
data.description: Derived principle: invidia (envy) is the capital vice of sadness at another's excellence or happiness, distinct from righteous indignation at injustice; it tends toward detraction, schadenfreude, and hostility.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Clear parallel with envy as analyzed in philosophy and psychology; theological packaging adds metaphysical claims not all accept.

pros.claim: Captures a stable psychological pattern—resentment of comparative status—that corrodes communities.
pros.evidence: Social science and virtue ethics both study status competition and envy-driven behavior.

cons.claim: Can blur into legitimate desire for fairness or anger at undeserved privilege.
cons.evidence: Distinguishing envy from warranted protest against inequality requires careful moral analysis.

st-ii-ii-q36.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 36 (envy)

envy-psychology-overview.title: Envy and social comparison — psychological overview

envy-vs-justice-note.title: Envy, resentment, and egalitarian justice — conceptual distinctions

data.name: Gluttony (gula) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this tradition, gluttony is not only eating too much: it is inordinate desire in the realm of food and drink—quantity, delicacy, or ritual that disorders health, sobriety, or solidarity.
data.description: Derived principle: gula (gluttony) is the capital vice of intemperance in eating and drinking—classically including excessive concern for costly or refined fare, not merely caloric excess.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Temperance language remains intelligible in public health; gourmet culture and eating disorders complicate simple labeling.

pros.claim: Connects individual appetite to stewardship of health and shared meals as moral practice.
pros.evidence: Public health ethics and environmental food ethics echo concerns about excess and waste.

cons.claim: Risk of stigmatizing body size or poverty when the term gluttony is used loosely.
cons.evidence: Critics note that metabolic, economic, and psychological factors challenge one-size moral judgments about eating.

st-ii-ii-q148.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 148 (gluttony)

food-ethics-public-health.title: Food, temperance, and public health ethics — overview

gluttony-stigma-critique.title: Moral language, weight stigma, and eating behavior — critical discussion

data.name: Greed (avaritia) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this list, greed denotes a disordered love of possessing—holding or seeking wealth in a way that subordinates justice, charity, or the common good.
data.description: Derived principle: avaritia (greed or covetousness) is the capital vice of excessive attachment to material goods, including insatiable acquisition and hoarding, classically contrasted with liberality and justice.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Widely echoed in religious and secular critiques of exploitation; boundaries between prudent provision and disordered attachment remain debated.

pros.claim: Illuminates structural harms when acquisition eclipses duty to others.
pros.evidence: Traditions link greed to fraud, usury (in historical sense), neglect of the poor, and environmental overreach.

cons.claim: Risk of moralizing wealth without distinguishing legitimate enterprise, saving, and innovation.
cons.evidence: Market societies debate when profit-seeking is productive versus exploitative; blanket talk of greed can oversimplify.

ccc-2536.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church — on covetousness and the tenth commandment (paragraph 2536)

st-ii-ii-q118.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 118 (avarice)

economic-ambiguity-note.title: Profit, virtue, and greed in market ethics — introductory discussion

data.name: Lust (luxuria) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this tradition, lust denotes sexual desire disordered by object, circumstance, or intent—treating persons as mere means to appetite.
data.description: Derived principle: luxuria (lust) is the capital vice of inordinate sexual appetite—desire that ignores temperance, consent, covenant, or the integral good of persons, as classically articulated in Christian sexual ethics.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: The category is central in traditional manuals of moral theology; modern disputes over consent, marriage, and autonomy make application highly contested.

pros.claim: Highlights objectification and appetite-driven harm that many ethical frameworks also condemn.
pros.evidence: Overlaps with secular concerns about exploitation, coercion, and pornography's incentives.

cons.claim: Traditional definitions often clash with contemporary views on sexual autonomy, LGBTQ dignity, and plural family forms.
cons.evidence: Ongoing moral and legal debates show deep disagreement on what counts as disordered versus healthy desire.

ccc-2351.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church — lust and chastity (paragraph 2351)

st-ii-ii-q153.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 153 (lust)

sexual-ethics-pluralism-note.title: Pluralism in sexual ethics — survey and critique

data.name: Pride (superbia) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In the classic list, pride is the disordered elevation of self—elevating the self above God, truth, or the good of others.
data.description: Derived principle from Christian moral tradition: pride (superbia) is a root distortion of self-love—excessive esteem for oneself, contempt for dependence on God or others—often treated as ordering or amplifying other vices.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Stable as a category within centuries of Christian theology and spiritual literature; secular or interfaith readers may reject the metaphysical framing while recognizing hubris as a moral phenomenon.

pros.claim: Names a recurring moral failure—hubris—that appears across cultures and institutions.
pros.evidence: Philosophy and literature independently criticize arrogance, self-deception, and contempt for limits; the tradition gives these a structured place.

cons.claim: Can be misread to condemn healthy self-respect or legitimate ambition.
cons.evidence: Pastoral and feminist critiques warn that pride language has sometimes been used to suppress dignity and assertiveness among the oppressed.

ccc-1866.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church — on vices and sins (paragraph 1866)

st-ii-ii-q162.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 162 (pride)

pastoral-caution-pride.title: Pastoral and ethical literature on dignity vs. disordered pride (overview)

data.name: Sloth (acedia) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this list, sloth is not mere laziness: it is spiritual apathy—refusal of the good one owes, especially toward God and neighbor.
data.description: Derived principle: acedia (sloth) is the capital vice of spiritual torpor or sorrow at the demands of the good—classically distinct from clinical depression, though the two raise difficult pastoral and medical questions.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Rich in monastic literature; modern readers often confuse acedia with laziness or depression, requiring careful interpretation.

pros.claim: Names civic and relational failure when people withdraw from obligations they could meet.
pros.evidence: Parallel discussions exist in virtue ethics (effort, diligence) and organizational ethics (negligence).

cons.claim: Moral language of sloth can blame victims of depression, burnout, or structural barriers.
cons.evidence: Mental health and disability advocates caution against spiritualizing illness or exhaustion.

st-ii-ii-q35.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 35 (acedia / sloth)

acedia-monastic-literature.title: Acedia in desert monastic sources — scholarly overview

acedia-depression-distinction.title: Spiritual acedia and clinical depression — pastoral and ethical boundaries

data.name: Wrath (ira) as capital vice
data.plainSummary: In this list, wrath denotes unjust anger—desire for vengeance or cruelty out of proportion to a real or perceived wrong.
data.description: Derived principle: ira (wrath or anger as vice) is the capital vice of disordered anger—resentment, rage, or cruelty that seeks harm beyond just defense or proportionate correction; classically distinguished from righteous anger at genuine injustice.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Anger's moral status is debated everywhere; tradition's distinction between ordered and disordered anger remains useful but not universally accepted.

pros.claim: Tracks cycles of retaliation and dehumanization familiar in criminal and political life.
pros.evidence: Restorative justice and conflict theory both study how unchecked anger entrenches harm.

cons.claim: Anger is sometimes a fitting response to oppression; labeling it wrath can silence legitimate outrage.
cons.evidence: Liberation ethics and social movements debate when anger is prophetic versus destructive.

st-ii-ii-q158.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 158 (anger)

wrath-and-justice-movements.title: Prophetic anger and social justice — ethical perspectives

data.name: Common law method
data.description: Much of U.S. law (especially in contracts, torts, property, and procedure) develops through judicial decisions that articulate, distinguish, and incrementally reshape rules—alongside statutes and constitutions.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Descriptive of large swaths of state and federal practice, though modern codes and regulations narrow its domain in many fields.

pros.claim: Allows law to adapt flexibly to new facts and evolving norms without waiting for comprehensive legislation.
pros.evidence: Judge-made doctrines continue to govern many private-law disputes and procedural details.

cons.claim: Can obscure clear rules, increase litigation costs, and yield uneven development across jurisdictions.
cons.evidence: Forum variation and complex multi-factor tests are common criticisms in tort and contract doctrine.

jurisdictions.citation: Mixed state and federal court development; no single enactment date

common-law-complexity-critique.title: Complexity and variation in common law doctrines — introductory note

data.name: Constitutional supremacy
data.description: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; inconsistent statutes and other government acts yield to it (including state law under the Supremacy Clause).
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Expressly stated in Article VI; uniformly treated as bedrock in federal jurisprudence.

pros.claim: Creates a single hierarchy of norms so rights and structural limits are not overridden by ordinary politics alone.
pros.evidence: Judicial invalidation of conflicting enactments is treated as a normal mechanism for enforcing written limits.

cons.claim: Shifts contentious value questions into constitutional interpretation, sometimes amplifying judicial power and social polarization.
cons.evidence: High-stakes disputes often turn on contested readings of open-textured provisions.

art-vi-supremacy.title: U.S. Constitution, Article VI, Clause 2 (Supremacy Clause)

constitutional-polarization-note.title: Constitutional politics and interpretive disagreement — introductory note

data.name: Due process of law
data.description: Due process requires government to follow fair procedures—and in substantive strands, to respect certain baseline protections—before depriving persons of life, liberty, or property (Fifth Amendment as to federal power; Fourteenth as to states).
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Deeply embedded in federal and state practice; central to modern rights litigation.

pros.claim: Guards against arbitrary punishment, secret proceedings, and capricious administrative action.
pros.evidence: Procedural requirements such as notice and hearing are standard features of deprivation scenarios.

cons.claim: Open-ended phrasing invites wide judicial discretion and disagreement over what process is due and what substance is protected.
cons.evidence: Long-running doctrinal splits over incorporation, fundamental rights, and administrative due process.

jurisdictions.citation: U.S. Const. amends. V, XIV, Section 1

fifth-fourteenth-due-process.title: U.S. Constitution, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments (Due Process Clauses)

due-process-open-texture.title: Due process doctrine — variability and debate

data.name: Equal protection of the laws
data.description: The Equal Protection Clause bars states from denying any person within their jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws; classifications among persons require justification by standards that vary with the context and the right at stake.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Core Fourteenth Amendment strand driving anti-discrimination and classification review.

pros.claim: Provides a constitutional lever against invidious discrimination and arbitrary class legislation.
pros.evidence: Used to invalidate or strictly scrutinize discriminatory state action across domains.

cons.claim: Tiered scrutiny and malleable standards generate persistent uncertainty and high-stakes judicial balancing.
cons.evidence: Ongoing doctrinal controversy over which groups and interests trigger which level of review.

fourteenth-equal-protection.title: U.S. Constitution, Fourteenth Amendment, Section 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

equal-protection-scrutiny-debate.title: Equal protection tiers of scrutiny — overview

data.name: Federalism (division of sovereign authority)
data.description: Sovereignty is split between a national government and the states: each has distinct lawmaking and enforcement domains, with federal law supreme only within enumerated federal powers.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Structurally embedded in the Constitution's enumeration of powers and the Tenth Amendment's reservation to the states.

pros.claim: Allows policy experimentation and local responsiveness while preserving a unified national sphere for certain matters.
pros.evidence: Historical variation among state laws alongside nationwide regimes in areas of federal competence.

cons.claim: Produces overlapping regulation, forum-shopping, and recurring uncertainty about the scope of federal versus state authority.
cons.evidence: Long-running litigation over Commerce Clause and preemption illustrates boundary disputes.

jurisdictions.citation: U.S. Const. amends. X; structural provisions art. I–III

tenth-amendment-overview.title: Tenth Amendment — powers reserved to the states

federalism-boundary-tension.title: Federalism and overlapping jurisdiction — introductory note

data.name: Judicial review
data.description: Courts may assess whether statutes and executive actions comply with the Constitution and refuse to enforce those that do not—tying the written constitution to ordinary adjudication.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Long treated as settled in federal practice since early 19th-century precedent, though its scope and legitimacy remain debated in theory.

pros.claim: Gives bite to constitutional limits that might otherwise be ignored by political majorities.
pros.evidence: Invalidation of unconstitutional enactments is a routine part of federal and state court practice.

cons.claim: Places major policy outcomes in the hands of unelected judges, raising democratic legitimacy and restraint debates.
cons.evidence: Scholarly and popular controversy over countermajoritarian difficulty and interpretive methodology.

countermajoritarian-debate.title: Judicial review and democratic theory — introductory note

data.name: Rule of law
data.description: Government officials—including law enforcement and courts—are bound by law; powers are exercised through known rules and procedures rather than arbitrary will, supporting predictability and accountability.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Widely invoked across U.S. legal culture as an ideal, though its content is contested and partially enforced through many distinct doctrines.

pros.claim: Anchors legitimacy in public norms that constrain coercion and protect expectations.
pros.evidence: Constitutional limits, administrative procedure, and judicial review are often framed as rule-of-law mechanisms.

cons.claim: The phrase is capacious enough to be used rhetorically on opposing sides of the same dispute.
cons.evidence: Competing invocations in debates over discretion, emergencies, and enforcement priorities.

jurisdictions.citation: Cross-cutting theme; not a single clause

data.name: Separation of powers
data.description: Legislative, executive, and judicial functions are assigned to distinct branches at the federal level, with checks and balances intended to prevent concentrated power and arbitrary rule.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Explicit in Articles I–III; treated as a core structural principle in U.S. constitutional doctrine.

pros.claim: Reduces the risk that a single actor can make, enforce, and interpret law without accountability from other branches.
pros.evidence: Institutional design allocates distinct core functions and inter-branch checks.

cons.claim: Can slow decision-making and invite branch conflict, gridlock, or emergency-power stretching of formal lines.
cons.evidence: Recurring debates over war powers, appointments, and enforcement discretion illustrate friction.

data.name: Stare decisis (respect for precedent)
data.description: Courts generally follow prior decisions on the same legal question to promote stability, reliance, and equal treatment—while allowing rare departures when precedent is unworkable or egregiously wrong.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Strong norm in appellate practice, though the Supreme Court has articulated exceptions and occasionally overturns landmark precedents.

pros.claim: Supports predictability for individuals, institutions, and markets that order conduct around prior holdings.
pros.evidence: Routine lower-court adherence to controlling precedent is expected absent distinguishing facts.

cons.claim: Can entrench mistaken or morally outdated decisions until a court is willing to bear the costs of reversal.
cons.evidence: High-profile overrulings illustrate tension between stability and correction.

jurisdictions.citation: See e.g. Planned Parenthood of Se. Pa. v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833 (1992) (stare decisis factors)

data.name: US Right to Try Act
data.description: Enacted federal law that allows terminally ill patients to access experimental treatments that have completed Phase I clinical trials but are not yet FDA-approved.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Broadly supported across party lines; some concerns from FDA about safety oversight gaps.

pros.claim: Expands patient autonomy over their own medical decisions at end of life.
pros.evidence: Consistent with Cruzan v. Director, MDH (1990) establishing right to refuse treatment, logically extendable to right to pursue treatment.

pros.claim: Provides hope and options where none previously existed within the regulatory framework.
pros.evidence: Prior to the act, expanded access (compassionate use) required lengthy FDA review averaging 4+ months.

cons.claim: May expose vulnerable patients to ineffective or harmful treatments without adequate safety data.
cons.evidence: Phase I trials establish basic safety but not efficacy; only ~10% of Phase I drugs reach approval.

cons.claim: Could undermine clinical trial enrollment if patients can access drugs outside trials.
cons.evidence: Some researchers report difficulty recruiting for Phase II/III trials in therapeutic areas where Right to Try is active.
